subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 3-year-old boy with developmental delay undergoes whole-exome sequencing. A synonymous variant is found in a neuronally expressed gene: the third nucleotide of a codon is changed, but the encoded amino acid is unchanged. The geneticist explains that the same amino acid can be specified by several codons and that a single tRNA can often read more than one of them.
question: Which of the following best explains this phenomenon?

options.text: The genetic code is overlapping, so one nucleotide participates in several codons
The genetic code is ambiguous, so one codon can specify several amino acids
Wobble base pairing allows the third nucleotide of the codon to vary while the first two determine specificity
The code is read in triplets, which prevents any change in the third position
The code is universal, so bacterial and human tRNAs are interchangeable

explanation_correct: The first two nucleotides of a codon pair strictly with the anticodon and largely determine which amino acid is specified, whereas the third nucleotide can form nonstandard (wobble) base pairs. This flexibility allows a single tRNA to recognize multiple synonymous codons and explains why many point mutations in the third position are silent. The genetic code is degenerate but unambiguous.

explanation_incorrect.A: The code is not overlapping; each nucleotide is read in only one codon.
explanation_incorrect.B: The code is unambiguous, meaning a given codon specifies only one amino acid.
explanation_incorrect.D: Triplet reading does not prevent changes in the third position; wobble permits them.
explanation_incorrect.E: The genetic code is nearly universal, but tRNAs are species-specific and are not interchangeable in this way.

educationalObjective: Wobble base pairing at the third codon position accounts for the degeneracy of the genetic code and for silent mutations.
